newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Earth Summit official says follow-up disappointing.
newsitem.headline: Earth Summit official says follow-up disappointing.

text.p: Maurice Strong, Secretary-General of the 1992 Earth Summit, said on Tuesday some progress had occurred in the ensuing four years but on the whole, environmental deterioration had worsened.
Four years after the Rio de Janeiro summit, there is evidence of moves towards eco-efficency in energy use, Strong said in a speech.
"But they are not happening on the scale required. On the whole, the deterioration of the environment has actually worsened."

Noting that the commitments in Rio were not legally binding, Strong said at a news conference after his speech that he wants to see an Earth Charter or People's Charter that relies on people power to hold governments accountable to promises made to protect the environment.
"Until a global system of legal enforcement exists, we have to rely on citizen power," said Strong.
He added he was worried that targets penned in Rio, notably in the reduction of carbon dioxide, were not achieved.
"These targets were modest, yet not achieved. My overall assessment of Rio is there are improvements yet not much gains."

Japan and Singapore were cited favourably by Strong for giving official development assistance for the commitments made in Rio, but he said funds promised during the summit had generally not been forthcoming.
He also said Rio was successful in creating local "Agendas 21" in some 1,600 cities, bringing global environmental issue down to ground levels.
Agenda 21, a document approved in Rio, is a comprehensive action plan on sustainable development to guide policies of governments into the next century.

But Strong said he was disappointed with the follow-up by most governments after Rio and many issues were stil unresolved, including the urgent need to reduce global carbon dioxide emission to avoid climate change.
He also called for a more equitable use of energy resources to ensure stability of the environment.
"Our present industrial system is not viable. It must change," Strong said. "It is like a cancer killing away the vital organs of our society...which may well be irreversible."

He said energy consumption in Asia is growing faster than in any OECD country. A recent report by the World Energy Council estimated that by 2020, developing countries will need some US$30 trillion in energy resources.
Strong called for greater cooperation between developing and industrialised countries, with the rich prepared to share in solving environmental problems of the poor.
"We really need a change in ethos and culture. We need to move from a culture of greed and competition to one of cooperation and stewardship, a culture of sharing," Strong said.
